In early 2026, figure skater Alysa Liu win Olympic gold and became a media sensation for the year that followed. My socials have been inundated with her inspiring comeback story, iconic halo hair, and everything in between.

What has intrigued me the most is the relationship she has with her name. She shares a first name with me and also has a surname of Chinese origin. For her, the y in Alysa is a long-ee /iː/ sound for her family; a short-i /ɪ/ for the media. The Liu is /ljoʊ/ for her family, and /luː/ for the press.

I have been entertained watching the internet argue how to pronounce Alysa Liu's name, even though Alysa Liu herself is receptive to several pronunciations. It's a debate I'm familiar with, as I pronounce my name, Alysa, as /ə'liːsə/ with the long-ee /iː/ sound.

I am accustomed to people writing and saying my name many ways. Baristas write Alyssa, Elissa, Elisa, Eliza, Allysa, Alicia, or Alisa on my drink cups. Professors would read Alysa as Alyssa, with the short-i /ɪ/, or Eliza, with the /aɪ/ diphthong. The language of names is inconsistent, messy, and beautiful.

My take is similar to Icelandic singer Laufey's 1 comments on her own name: "I'd rather have you pronounce it wrong than not pronounce it at all." I'll turn my head when someone utters three syllables that begin and end with a schwa /ə/.

In May 2026, I ordered a Starbucks Caramel Macchiato. For the first time, it was spelt correctly: Alysa. It's difficult to attribute the impact of the Alysa Liu's fame on the pronunciation of my name. So out of curiosity, I started tracking how baristas spell and call my name when I order drinks. Here's some nice visualizations of my Starbucks ordering habits and interactions. Some people ask about spelling, denoted by [Asked].

I have also created this interactive chart in Vega/Altair.
